metaDescription: Six Dolphin pool robots compared: Escape, Nautilus AG, CC Plus Wi-Fi, Titan and the cordless EON 100 and 120D, with filters, cables and upkeep.
expertTake: The Nautilus CC Plus Wi-Fi is the sensible choice for most in-ground pools because it adds scheduling to a proven corded design. The Escape is the value pick for owners who want a plain robot, and anyone who hates lifting should prefer the cordless EON line or a caddy.
introParagraphs: This maker has built its reputation on corded robots with active scrubbing brushes, top-loading filters and simple plug-in operation. More recent models add phone control and a few cordless designs, so the range now spans very different ownership styles.

The model names look similar, which makes the decision tricky. What really separates them is whether the machine is built for above-ground or in-ground pools, how it is powered, and whether you want scheduling from a phone.

products.name: Dolphin Nautilus CC Plus Wi-Fi with universal caddy

specList.label: Control
specList.value: Wi-Fi scheduling in the maker's app

products.description:
Think of the CC Plus Wi-Fi as the established corded design with a phone attached. The cable supplies power from a transformer on the deck, so there is no battery to age, and the active scrubbing brush works the surface as the machine climbs walls. The Wi-Fi link lets you set a schedule or start a cycle from the house, which the older plain models cannot do.

The included universal caddy is a bigger deal than it sounds, because a wet robot is heavy and awkward to carry. Compared with the Nautilus Titan above it in cost, the CC Plus Wi-Fi leaves out the waterline-focused scrubbing and the multi-layer filter, so it fits owners who do not fight a scum ring. The cable can twist, so uncoil it on the deck and let it hang straight.

Expect to rinse the top-load basket after every run, a job that takes a minute. Keep the transformer sheltered from rain and sun. The brush and tracks are the wear items to watch by year three.
products.bestFor: In-ground pool owners who want a proven corded robot with phone scheduling.
pros: Corded power means no battery pack to wear out
Wi-Fi scheduling starts cycles from inside the house
Caddy turns a heavy wet robot into a rolling job
Active brush and top-load basket keep upkeep simple
cons: Cable can twist and tangle on busy pool layouts
No dedicated waterline scrub on this model
Costs more than the plain corded models

products.name: Dolphin Nautilus Titan Wi-Fi with waterline scrubbing

specList.label: Retrieval
specList.value: Pick-up mode waits at the water edge

products.description:
The Titan is the machine to look at when the waterline is the problem. It adds a wall-to-waterline scrub to the corded platform, so the ring of oil and sunscreen at the surface gets attention each cycle. A multi-layer filter stack sits behind the intake to catch finer material than a single basket.

Its pick-up mode parks the robot at the water edge when the cycle ends, so you lift it from the deck instead of reaching for the cable. That is a real convenience for anyone with a bad back. Against the Nautilus CC Plus Wi-Fi it is the more capable and more expensive machine, and the extra cost only pays off if waterline cleaning matters to you.

A multi-layer filter needs more frequent rinsing than a single basket, so budget a few minutes after each run. Check the app after firmware updates to confirm the schedule survived. Coil the cable on the deck between uses.
products.bestFor: Pools with a stubborn waterline ring and owners who want easy pickup.
pros: Waterline scrubbing targets the oil and sunscreen ring
Multi-layer filter catches finer material than one basket
Pick-up mode brings the robot to the water edge
App scheduling fits a daily routine
cons: Highest cost in this Dolphin lineup
Layered filter needs more frequent rinsing
Corded design still means cable management

products.name: Dolphin Nautilus AG corded for above-ground pools

specList.label: Setup
specList.value: Plug in, drop in the water, press start

products.description:
The Nautilus AG is the only model here named for its pool type. Above-ground pools have shallower, softer walls and often vinyl liners, and a robot designed for them keeps the climb gentle. The active scrubbing brush works against the liner, which is why gentle matters.

Setup is as plain as it gets: plug in the transformer, drop the robot in, press start. That simplicity is the selling point, since there is no app, no battery and no pairing. Compared with the Escape, which also lists above-ground use, the AG is the machine with a clearer pedigree for that pool type, though both do the basics.

Rinse the top-load basket after each run and inspect the brush for wear, since a worn brush is the most likely cause of liner scuffing. Store it out of the sun, and keep the cable loosely coiled. Because above-ground pools are easy to drain and refill, a quick check for hair around the tracks is worth the thirty seconds.
products.bestFor: Above-ground and vinyl-liner pools where simplicity matters.
pros: Built for the softer, shallower walls of above-ground pools
Plug-and-play setup with no app or pairing
Active brush scrubs the liner surface
Top-load basket empties in seconds
cons: No scheduling, so each run is manual
Not the machine for deep in-ground walls

products.name: Dolphin Escape with HyperBrush and oversized cartridge

specList.label: Debris cartridge
specList.value: Oversized, up to 60 percent more capacity

products.description:
The Escape is the budget entry that still carries the brand's key hardware: a HyperBrush roller, continuous HyperGrip tracks and a debris cartridge the maker says holds up to 60 percent more than its older design. Two low-voltage DC motors split drive and suction, which is gentler on the electrical side of the pool. It lists suitability for both above-ground and in-ground pools.

The tradeoff is features. There is no phone control and no waterline brush, so you set it by hand and clean the ring yourself. Against the Nautilus AG, the Escape claims more flexibility on pool type but less specialization. A large cartridge means fewer stops to empty it in leaf season.

Upkeep centers on the cartridge, which should be emptied and rinsed after every run. The tracks pick up hair, so check them monthly. Because it is the least costly Dolphin, treat it as a workhorse and keep a spare cartridge if you can find one.
products.bestFor: Owners who want a basic corded Dolphin at the lowest cost in the range.
pros: Oversized cartridge reduces emptying stops in leaf season
HyperGrip tracks grip wet walls well
Low-voltage DC motors split drive and suction
Lists both above-ground and in-ground compatibility
cons: Entry model has the fewest conveniences

products.name: Dolphin Nautilus EON 120D cordless, 4.5 hours
products.description:
The EON 120D is the longest-running cordless Dolphin on this list, with a stated 4.5 hours and multiple modes including floor-only and waterline-only. That runtime gives margin for a pool up to fifty feet long, which is the size the maker names. Wi-Fi control lets you schedule and monitor it from the house.

It costs noticeably more than the plain corded Dolphins, and a lithium pack is the price of freedom from the cable. Compared with the EON 100 it nearly doubles the stated run window, so it suits larger pools. Battery capacity will decline over several seasons, so the runtime figure is a new-pack number.

Charge after every run and store the robot shaded, because heat is the battery's worst enemy. The filter basket needs a rinse each time. Confirm the retrieval method before buying, since a heavy wet cordless unit is still a lift.
products.bestFor: Pools up to fifty feet that need long cordless cycles.
pros: Long stated runtime covers a fifty-foot pool
Separate waterline-only mode targets the scum ring
Wi-Fi app handles scheduling and status
No cable to twist or trip over
cons: Lithium pack fades over several seasons
Costs well above the plain corded models
Wet cordless body is still heavy to lift

products.name: Dolphin Nautilus EON 100 cordless, 2.5 hours
products.description:
The EON 100 is the smaller, shorter-running sibling of the EON 120D. A stated 2.5 hours of runtime is enough for a typical residential pool when the water is clean, and the machine still climbs walls and scrubs the waterline. It brings the same Wi-Fi app and the same pool size claim of up to fifty feet.

The compromise is time. On a leafy pool, 2.5 hours can run out before the job is done, and the robot will park mid-cycle. Against the Nautilus CC Plus Wi-Fi, it trades unlimited corded runtime for tangle-free convenience.

Plan a charge after each run and shade it between uses. Keep an eye on the brush and tracks each season. If your pool is large or dirty, step up to the EON 120D instead of asking this model to carry the load.
products.bestFor: Smaller, cleaner pools where cordless convenience matters more than endurance.
pros: Cordless freedom with wall and waterline cleaning
Wi-Fi app schedules and monitors cycles
Lower cost than the EON 120D
Suits pools up to the maker's fifty-foot figure
cons: 2.5 hours can fall short on large or leafy pools
Fewer cleaning modes than the EON 120D

buyingCriteria.explanation: Dolphin sells corded models like the Nautilus CC Plus Wi-Fi and Titan alongside cordless ones like the EON 100 and EON 120D. Corded designs never run out of power and have no battery to replace, while cordless ones remove the tangle. The EON 100 lists 2.5 hours and the EON 120D lists 4.5 hours, and both figures assume a clean pool. Pick corded for large or daily-use pools and cordless for convenience.

The Nautilus AG is built for above-ground pools while most others target in-ground ones. The Escape lists both. An above-ground model in a deep in-ground pool will struggle on walls. Check the maker's stated pool type and size, especially the fifty-foot figure on the EON models.

The Titan and EON 120D list waterline scrubbing, while the Escape and AG do not. A dedicated waterline brush keeps the oil ring in check. Without it you scrub by hand. Decide how much that ring bothers you before paying more.

The CC Plus Wi-Fi, Titan and EON models use an app to schedule runs. The AG and Escape are strictly manual. Scheduling is a convenience, not a cleaning upgrade. Confirm the basic run still works if the phone link fails.

Most Dolphins load from the top, which makes rinsing quick. The Titan adds a multi-layer filter that catches finer dirt but needs more frequent cleaning. The Escape offers an oversized cartridge that holds more debris. Match the filter to your debris and your patience.

The Titan's pick-up mode parks the robot at the water edge, and the CC Plus Wi-Fi ships with a caddy. A wet robot is heavy, so retrieval matters for anyone with back or shoulder limits. Weigh these conveniences against raw cleaning specs.

specDecoder.meaning: The maximum pool length the maker supports. Cable length or battery limits this number.
specDecoder.watchFor: Both EON models list pools up to fifty feet.

specDecoder.meaning: A stacked filter that traps coarse and fine debris separately. It improves water clarity but clogs faster.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Titan uses one, so plan for frequent rinses.

specDecoder.meaning: A routine that parks the robot at the water edge at the end of a cycle. It reduces lifting from the deep end.

howWeEvaluated.title: Power platform
howWeEvaluated.description: We separated corded and cordless designs and compared stated runtime. The EON 120D at 4.5 hours led the cordless range. We weighed battery wear against cable tangles.

howWeEvaluated.title: Pool type fit
howWeEvaluated.description: We matched each model to the pool type the maker states. The Nautilus AG stood out for above-ground use. We flagged size limits like the fifty-foot figure.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cleaning coverage
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked waterline and wall claims on each listing. The Titan and EON 120D led on waterline. We treated these as maker claims.

howWeEvaluated.title: Filter design
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared top-load baskets, the Titan's multi-layer stack and the Escape's oversized cartridge. Ease of access counted. We rewarded filters you will actually rinse.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership burden
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at caddies, pick-up mode and cable handling. Dolphin's published cycle times and filter details, read next to what owners report, back up these notes. Lifting and storage counted for older owners.

howToChoose.note: The EON 120D sits near the top; check the listing for current pricing.

cards.label: Corded (CC Plus Wi-Fi, Titan, AG, Escape)
cards.text: Unlimited runtime, no battery to replace and proven designs. The cable can tangle. Best for big pools and daily use.

cards.label: Cordless (EON 100, EON 120D)
cards.text: No cable and easy drop-in. Runtime fades as the pack ages, and the 2.5 hour EON 100 can run short. Best for moderate pools.

howToChoose.note: Big pool or daily runs, go corded. Convenience on a moderate pool, go cordless.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Look for pick-up mode, a caddy or surface parking. Lifting a wet robot is the hardest part of ownership. Cable length matters less than a way to get the robot out.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Titan parks at the water edge and the CC Plus Wi-Fi ships with a caddy. The EON models skip the cable altogether.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You fight a waterline ring or want phone control. The Titan and CC Plus Wi-Fi add those. A bigger pool justifies the EON 120D.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Your pool is simple and you do not mind pressing start. The Escape or AG covers it, and the money buys spare parts.

maintenance.why: Dried debris clogs mesh. A rinse keeps suction steady.
A twisted cable kinks and wears the swivel. Straightening it extends life.

maintenance.interval: After each run on EON models
maintenance.why: Heat and deep discharge age lithium cells. Shade keeps capacity.
Worn brushes scuff liners and tracks lose grip. Replacement parts are cheaper than liner repair.
Fine layers clog quickly. A clogged stack strains the motor.

faq.q: Which Dolphin is best for most pools?
faq.a: The Nautilus CC Plus Wi-Fi suits most in-ground pools because it adds scheduling to a proven design. Move up to the Titan for a waterline ring. Choose the AG for an above-ground pool.

Cordless removes cable tangles and eases storage, but the battery fades over seasons. The EON 120D at 4.5 hours handles larger pools, while the EON 100 suits smaller ones. Corded models never run out of charge.
No. Wi-Fi is a scheduling convenience, not a cleaning upgrade. The AG and Escape run fine without it. Confirm basic controls work if the link fails.
It keeps the key hardware but drops scheduling and waterline scrubbing. That is a fair tradeoff for a simple pool. It is a good workhorse.
Corded models can run many seasons with brush and track replacement. Cordless ones are limited by the battery pack. Parts availability from the maker is a strength.

faq.q: Do robots replace the pool filter?
faq.a: No. They collect debris in their own basket and ease the load on your main filter. They do not circulate or sanitize water.
